disclaimer.summary: This content was researched from published ITF-affiliated sources and is provided as general educational guidance, not an official syllabus.
disclaimer.detail: ITF Taekwon-Do has been governed by multiple separate organisations since a split in 2002, and individual schools set their own exact syllabus, technique lists, and time-in-grade requirements. The belt-colour meanings below are consistently reproduced across independent ITF-affiliated sources and are quoted from General Choi Hong Hi's writings. The grading structure describes the general pattern used across ITF schools; always confirm the exact requirements for your own grading with your instructor.

beltMeanings.meaning: Signifies innocence, as that of the beginning student who has no previous knowledge of Taekwon-Do.
Signifies the earth, from which a plant sprouts and takes root, as the Taekwon-Do foundation is being laid.
Signifies the plant's growth, as Taekwon-Do skills begin to develop.
Signifies the sky and the heavens, towards which the plant matures into a tree, as training in Taekwon-Do progresses.
Signifies danger, cautioning the student to exercise control and warning the opponent to stay away.
The opposite of white, therefore signifying maturity and proficiency in Taekwon-Do, and the wearer's imperviousness to darkness and fear.

beltMeaningsSource.attribution: Reproduced from General Choi Hong Hi's "Taekwon-Do" (The Condensed Encyclopedia)

gradingStructure.description: Demonstrating the new pattern for the grade being tested, plus some or all previously learned patterns.
Stances, blocks, strikes, punches, and kicks performed individually or as line-work combinations, testing precision and control.
Pre-arranged sparring with a partner, starting at 3-step sparring for beginners and progressing to 2-step and 1-step sparring at higher grades.
Semi-free and free sparring, introduced partway through the colour belts and expanding in intensity and format at black belt.
Releases from grabs and holds, introduced partway through the colour belts and expanded with takedowns and multiple-attacker scenarios at black belt.
Board breaking to demonstrate technique power, introduced from black tag (1st Kup) onward.
Korean terminology, belt-colour meanings, the Student Oath and Tenets, and ITF history and founder facts, with depth increasing at each grade.
A minimum training period between gradings that increases with rank, from roughly a few months between early colour belts to 18+ months between dan grades.

tiers.focus: Foundational stances, the four-directional punch and block drills (Saju Jirugi, Saju Makgi), and basic etiquette. No sparring or breaking yet.
First pattern, Chon-Ji. Introduction to 3-step pre-arranged sparring.
Second pattern, Dan-Gun. Continued fundamentals and 3-step sparring.
Third pattern, Do-San. Expanding technique vocabulary and combinations.
Fourth pattern, Won-Hyo. 3-step sparring sequences continue, semi-free sparring introduced.
Fifth pattern, Yul-Gok. One-step sparring and free sparring introduced, along with self-defence release techniques.
Sixth pattern, Joong-Gun. Continued sparring and self-defence development.
Seventh pattern, Toi-Gye. Increasing sparring intensity and technique combinations.
Eighth pattern, Hwa-Rang. More advanced self-defence and sparring scenarios.
Ninth pattern, Choong-Moo. Breaking (power test) introduced, along with a longer minimum training period before the Black Belt grading.

All colour-belt patterns plus a new dan-level pattern, advanced sparring (including 2-on-1 free sparring), multi-attacker self-defence, breaking, a written theory essay, and a grading panel of senior ITF examiners. Time between dan grades increases substantially with rank.
